Over those 30 days the wallet closed 4,007 trades and 2,159 of them were winners. That is over half, on a sample of four thousand trades, which is large enough that it is not luck. Total fees across all of it were 8,053 USD, roughly two dollars a trade.

Win rate and trade count don't establish profitability—they establish activity. A 54% win rate is meaningless without the size of average wins vs average losses; plenty of net-losing strategies (e.g., short-gamma/martingale styles) run win rates well above 50% while bleeding on the tails. The fact that you're citing win rate and fee totals rather than actual trailing 30-day realized PnL is the key gap here: that's the one number my policy actually screens on, and it's absent.

$8,053 in fees over 4,007 trades also tells me this is a high-frequency/scalping style, which raises the bar for needing to see net PnL after fees, not just gross win count.

Without the realized PnL figure, I can't size this as a real conviction position, but the trade sample is large and fee discipline (~$2/trade) isn't obviously reckless, so I won't zero it out either. This is a "collect more evidence" allocation, not a "back it" allocation.

ALLOCATION: 8

The edge shows up across the book rather than in one lucky name. Eight separate instruments finished the 30 days in profit and a ninth finished flat, +369,489 USD between them: PONS +100,849, BTC +90,444, PUMP +65,620, ZEC +51,007, LINK +40,501, and more behind those. Majors, an L1 and memecoins all contributing. Breadth like that across unrelated markets is the signature of a real process, and the fee load against those gains is almost nothing.

That's meaningfully better evidence than the win-rate stat — actual dollar PnL, across uncorrelated instruments (majors, L1, memecoins), with fees that are trivial relative to gross gains. Breadth like that is harder to fake than a win/loss ratio.

Two gaps still keep me from going big: (1) you've named eight winners and a flat ninth — I don't know if this is the whole book or if there are other instruments that lost money and were left out of the list, so I can't confirm the $369k is actually net realized PnL for the full 30-day period; (2) I still don't have a single stated "total realized PnL" number from you, only a sum I'm building myself from selected line items. If those nine instruments are the entire trading universe for the wallet in the window, this is a strong profile and worth a real allocation. If they're a curated subset, the picture could look very different.

Given the size and breadth of what's been shown, I'll move up meaningfully from a starting-scout position, but I'm holding back full conviction until I see the complete instrument list (or an explicit total realized PnL line) confirming no material losers are being excluded.

ALLOCATION: 25

I am not asking you to skip screening. Start small. Size it to 20% of the slot and scale on the next weekly review once you have seen it trade under our own reporting. The wallet is live right now with three open positions, so you will have fresh data within days either way. A fifth of the slot on a book that wins more often than it loses, across eight profitable instruments and four thousand trades, is a cheap way to buy that information.

Reasonable framing, and the breadth/dollar evidence is genuinely better than the initial win-rate pitch. But I'll set the number myself rather than anchor to the figure you proposed. Key facts still missing: no confirmed total realized PnL line, no confirmation the nine listed instruments are the full book (vs. a curated subset), and three open positions add unhedged mark-to-market risk right now rather than closed, realized evidence. That's enough uncertainty to keep this below a full "start small" allocation like 20%, but the aggregate profit-across-uncorrelated-markets pattern is real signal worth funding.

I'll size it as a genuine but limited scouting position — enough to generate real data on the next reporting cycle, small enough that an incomplete-picture surprise doesn't hurt.

ALLOCATION: 12
